A U T H O R ’ S D E S K 
Assalamu Alaikum, 
Writing this book has been a journey of both learning and reflection. My 
hope is that it serves as a bridge  connecting the timeless wisdom of the 
Prophet ﷺ with the challenges we face in our modern lives. 
Tibb an-Nabawi is not just about remedies or foods; it is a holistic 
approach to life that nurtures the body, heart, and soul. In compiling this 
work, I aimed to show how the guidance of the Prophet ﷺ preserved in

the Qur’an, Sunnah, and classical scholarship can be applied today, 
alongside what we now understand from modern science. 
My prayer is that this work becomes a source of benefit, that it reminds us 
of the mercy, wisdom, and care Allah has woven into our lives, and that it 
encourages us to live in harmony with His guidance. May Allah grant us 
health, ease our struggles, and make us among those who care for both our 
bodies and our souls. 
With gratitude and humility, 
Aisha Dahir

P R E FA C E 
All praise is due to Allah, the Lord of the worlds. May Peace and blessings be 
upon the Messenger Muhammad ﷺ, the seal of the Prophets, whose guidance 
touches every aspect of life, including the care of the body, mind, and soul. 
Have you ever woken up with a burning sensation in your stomach, struggled 
with constant fatigue, or felt frustrated because no remedy seemed to worked? 
Long before modern medicine, the prophet ﷺ taught approach to health, one

that includes body heart and soul together. The Prophet ﷺ said: 
"Allah has not sent down a disease except that He has also sent down its cure." 
(Ṣaḥih Muslim 2204) 
This simple yet profound hadith is the heartbeat of Prophetic Medicine. Every 
illness carries within it a cure, and every ailment is paired with a path toward 
healing both physical and spiritual. It reminds us that seeking treatment is not 
just permissible; it is part of living in harmony with the wisdom Allah has

placed in creation. 
Across centuries, humanity has sought remedies for its pains, from physical 
ailments to emotional struggles and spiritual unrest. Today, despite modern 
advancements, we face rising stress, lifestyle-related diseases, and a deep 
longing for holistic well-being. Many solutions focus only on the body, 
forgetting that true wellness Is born when heart, soul, and body are aligned. 
This book is an invitation to rediscover timeless wisdom: remedies that are

natural, accessible, and intimately connected with our spiritual well-being. It is 
about prevention, moderation, and trusting in Allah’s plan while taking steps 
toward health .In a world where many feel disconnected from what they eat, 
overwhelmed by stress, and desperate for holistic answers, Tibb an-Nabawi 
offers clarity, balance, and hope. Healing is not only about the body, it is about 
returning to the Sunnah aligning with nature. May Allah make this work a 
source of benefit. Amin

TA S AW W U F A N D T H E P S Y C H O L O G Y O F H E A L I N G 
The Forgotten Dimension 
When people think of medicine, they think of the body. But the Prophet ﷺ 
taught us that true health is holistic: body, heart, mind, and soul. 
Modern science calls it psychology. Islam calls it tazkiyah — the purification of 
the self. 
Tasawwuf = Cognitive Behavioral Therapy 
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) trains the mind to: 
•
Catch destructive thoughts. 
•
Question them. 
•

Catch destructive thoughts. 
•
Question them. 
•
Replace them with healthier beliefs. 
Centuries before CBT, tasawwuf taught: 
•
Muhāsabah → self-reckoning. 
•
Mujāhadah → struggling against the ego. 
•
Dhikr & tawakkul → anchoring the mind in Allah. 
Where psychology says “reframe the thought,” Islam says “purify the heart.” 
Prophetic Parenting & Emotional Wounds

“He is not of us who does not show mercy to children.” Sahih Muslim 2318a 
Prophetic parenting was trauma-informed long before psychology named it. 
Mercy prevents wounds that harden into depression and anxiety later in life.

Psychologists now say loneliness is deadlier than smoking.

Caring for neighbors.

The ummah itself is a healing system. No believer is meant to suffer in silence. 
The Qur’an: Emotional Balance 
Too much fear leads to despair. 
Too much hope leads to delusion. 
The Qur’an teaches balance: 
•
Fear keeps the soul alert. 
•
Hope keeps the soul alive.

Empathy as Medicine 
When the Prophet ﷺ felt sorrow, Allah revealed Surah ad-Ḍuḥā: 
“Did He not find you an orphan and shelter you?” 
The therapy was perspective + service: 
•
Remember blessings. 
•
Care for orphans. 
•
Serve the poor. 
The cure for sadness is not only reflection, but healing others. 
What psychology calls CBT, Islam calls tazkiyah.

What psychology calls CBT, Islam calls tazkiyah. 
What psychology calls resilience, the Qur’an calls sabr and shukr. 
What psychology calls trauma-informed parenting, the Sunnah calls rahmah. 
And what psychology calls nutritional psychiatry, Islam calls tibb an-nabawi. 
Tasawwuf heals the heart. Sunnah foods heal the body. Together, they restore 
harmony between mind, body, and soul.

F O U N D AT I O N S O F P R O P H E T I C M E D I C I N E 
1. The Philosophy of Healing in Islam 
Islam views health as an amanah (trust) from Allah, and medicine as part of 
divine mercy. The Qur’an itself establishes two categories of healing: 
1.
Spiritual healing: 
“And We send down in the Qur’an that which is a healing and a mercy 
for the believers…” (Qur’an 17:82) 
 
Healing here refers to diseases of the heart — arrogance, doubt, despair, 
envy — which no physical doctor can cure. 
2.

2.
Physical healing: 
“…and when I am ill, it is He who cures me.” (Qur’an 26:80) 
 
This emphasizes that while we use means (medicine, diet, treatment), 
Allah is the ultimate healer (Ash-Shāfī). 
Holistic Triad of Healing 
Imam Ibn al-Qayyim (d. 751H) in Zād al-Maʿad wrote: 
•
The body requires balance in diet, rest, and activity. 
•
The heart requires purification from sins. 
•
The soul requires attachment to Allah.

•
The soul requires attachment to Allah. 
This triad mirrors what modern medicine now calls the biopsychosocial 
model, recognizing that disease is rarely just physical, it involves 
psychological, environmental, and spiritual factors.

2. The Prophet ﷺ as the Physician of Body and Soul 
The Prophet ﷺ was not formally trained as a doctor, but his guidance in 
medicine reflects divine wisdom. He combined natural remedies, preventive 
habits, and spiritual cures. 
Lifestyle Preventive Sunnah 
•
Moderation in food: 
“The son of Adam does not fill a vessel worse than his stomach…” 
(Sinan Ibn majah 3349). 
Modern science affirms that overeating contributes to obesity, diabetes,

and cardiovascular disease. Caloric moderation extends lifespan in 
animals and is linked to longevity in humans. 
•
Hygiene: wuduʾ, siwak, ghusl, trimming nails, covering vessels at night. 
These habits prevented infectious disease long before germ theory 
(Pasteur, 19th century). 
•
Exercise & movement: The Prophet ﷺ raced with his wives, 
encouraged archery, horse riding, and swimming. Today, exercise is 
known to reduce chronic disease risk and improve mental health.

and prevention. 
3. Prophetic Medicine vs. Greek & Modern Medicine 
•
Greek tradition (Hippocrates, Galen) emphasized humors (blood, 
phlegm, yellow bile, black bile). Ibn Sina and al-Razi integrated this with 
Islamic thought. 
•
Modern medicine excels in surgery, pharmacology, and acute care — 
but often neglects prevention, diet, and spirituality. 
•
Prophetic Medicine focuses on balance, prevention, and aligning with 
nature, while keeping Allah as the true healer.

D O N O T T H R O W AWAY P O M E G R A N AT E P E E L S ! 
In Tibb al-Nabawi, the peel of the pomegranate (Qishr al-Rumman) is actually considered 
more medicinally potent than the fruit itself when it comes to "drying" and "firming" the 
body. While the seeds are a food, the peel is a powerful astringent, a substance that causes

tissues to contract. 
Ibn al-Qayyim and other classical physicians used it as a "tan" for the internal organs, similar 
to how leather is tanned to make it strong and water-resistant. 
1. Stomach and Digestive Ulcers 
The peel is a primary remedy for a "loose" or "weak" stomach. 
• The "Tanning" Effect: By boiling the peel and drinking the water, it helps tighten the 
stomach lining. This is used for those who suffer from chronic diarrhea or IBS

(Irritable Bowel Syndrome) where the stool is always watery. 
• Healing Ulcers: Its drying nature helps "close" internal wounds. Ibn al-Qayyim notes that 
it cleanses the stomach of "foul humors" and excess phlegm that cause nausea. 
2. Oral Health and Gums 
Because the peel is rich in tannins, it is an excellent natural remedy for the mouth. 
• Strengthening Gums: Boiling the peel and using the liquid as a mouthwash helps stop 
bleeding gums (gingivitis) and firms up "receding" gums.

• Bad Breath: It neutralizes the bacteria in the throat and stomach that cause foul odors, 
especially when the smell originates from a "moist" or acidic stomach. 
3. Women's Health (Drying Excess Moisture)

formation.

How to Prepare the Peel Remedy 
The Basic Decoction (Tea)

The Basic Decoction (Tea) 
1. Dry the Peels: Take the peels of a fresh pomegranate and let them dry in the sun or a low-
temperature oven until they are brittle. 
2. Boil: Add 1 tablespoon of dried, crushed peels to 2 cups of water. 
3. Simmer: Boil for about 10–15 minutes until the water turns a deep reddish-amber color. 
4. Usage: Drink: Half a cup for diarrhea or stomach ulcers (sweeten with honey to balance 
the bitterness). 
• Gargle: Use for throat or gum health.

The Powder Form 
You can grind the dried peels into a fine powder. 
• External Wounds: Sprinkle a tiny amount on weeping wounds to dry them out. 
• With Honey: Mix the powder with honey into a paste. Licking a small amount helps with 
sore throats and internal "heat."

thorn prick), as it cools the area and reduces the throbbing pain.

Ibn al-Qayyim clarifies that the use of Henna for headaches is a specific 
remedy based on the cause of the pain:

inflammation in the head. Because Henna is cold and dry, applying it to the

revelation often caused the Prophet ﷺ a heavy feverish sensation or headache; 
Henna acted as a cooling compress to stabilize the temperature. 
3. Clinical Benefits Summary 
According to Ibn al-Qayyim, Henna’s benefits extend to various parts of the 
body: 
 For the Mouth: Gargling with Henna or chewing its leaves helps treat mouth

ulcers, sores, and thrush in children.

blisters. In some narrations, companions reported that the Prophet ﷺ would 
advise anyone complaining of foot pain to apply Henna.

is not broken) as it prevents blistering by "firming" the skin layers. 
 For Smallpox: He mentions that applying Henna to the feet of a child in the

early stages of smallpox can help prevent the disease from spreading to the 
eyes. 
Medical Nuance: Ibn al-Qayyim notes that the choice of Henna depends on the 
temperament of the illness. Since Henna is cold, it is a "miracle cure" for hot, 
inflammatory ailments, but may not be as effective for "cold" or "congestive" 
headaches.

The Healing Powers of the Names of Allah 
Introduction 
The Names of Allah are more than words; they are manifestations of His 
attributes and realities that shape the universe. Allah says: 
“And to Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them.” 
(Surah al-A‘rāf 7:180) 
For centuries, believers have found peace, strength, and healing by 
remembering Allah through His Names. Recently, Dr. Ibrahim Karim, a

biologist and founder of the science of “BioGeometry,” conducted a three-year 
research project exploring how the recitation of Allah’s Names impacts the 
human body. His findings suggest that the Names of Allah influence the body’s 
bio-energy field, strengthening immunity and harmonizing inner balance. 
Scientific Discovery 
Dr. Karim employed precision methods to measure subtle energy fields in the 
body. He discovered that specific Names of Allah resonate with different

organs and systems, stimulating healing and restoring order. 
Among his findings: 
•
Ear – As-Samī‘ (The All-Hearing) 
•
Bone – An-Nāfi‘ (The Source of Benefit) 
•
Backbone – Al-Jabbār (The Compeller) 
•
Knee – Ar-Ra’ūf (The Clement) 
•
Heart – An-Nūr (The Light) 
•
Muscles – Al-Qawiyy (The All-Strong) 
•
Stomach – Ar-Razzāq (The Provider)

Kidney – Al-Ḥayy (The Ever-Living) 
•
Liver – An-Nāfi‘ (The Source of Benefit) 
•
Womb – Al-Khāliq (The Creator) 
•
Lung – Ar-Razzāq (The Sustainer) 
•
Thyroid & Arteries – Al-Jabbār (The Compeller) 
•
Migraine – Al-Ghaniyy (The Rich)

Cancer – Al-Jalīl (The Majestic) 
And many more correspondences across the human system. 
Spiritual Dimension 
For believers, this discovery is not surprising. The Qur’an already affirms that 
the remembrance of Allah heals and strengthens the heart:

“Indeed, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest.” 
(Surah ar-Ra‘d 13:28) 
When a believer calls upon Allah with His Names—whether saying Yā Shāfī 
(O Healer), Yā Qawiyy (O Strong), or Yā Nūr (O Light)—it is not only a 
spiritual act but also a form of medicine that harmonizes body and soul.

A simple way to integrate this into daily life is: 
1.
Identify the Name of Allah connected to your condition or area of 
weakness.

Reflection 
Healing is more than the absence of pain, it is the return of the soul to its Lord. 
Throughout this book, we have explored the many layers of shifā’ that Allah 
has gifted to mankind: the healing of the body through the foods and remedies 
of the Sunnah, the healing of the heart through the Qur’an and dhikr, and the 
healing of the soul through du‘ā and reliance upon Allah. 
Every cure ultimately comes from Allah alone. Medicines, herbs, and even the

recitation of His Beautiful Names are but means. The true Healer (Ash-Shāfī) is 
Allah, the One who created both the disease and the cure, the pain and the 
relief. 
Sometimes Allah heals us by removing the illness. Other times, He heals us by 
drawing us closer to Him through the illness. In both states, there is mercy, 
wisdom, and love. 
“And when I am ill, it is He who cures me.” (Surah Ash-Shu‘arā’ 26:80)

Balance (mīzān, ﻣﯿﺰان) is a foundational principle in the Qur’an, in nature, and 
in the healing traditions of Islamic medicine. Allah ﷻ says: 
“And the sky He has raised, and set the balance, so that you do not 
transgress in the balance.” 
(Qur’an 55:7–8) 
This verse teaches that every part of creation stars, seasons, winds, water, the

human body functions according to a precise balance. Just as the universe 
collapses when this balance is broken, the human body becomes ill when its 
inner balance is disturbed. 
Classical scholars of Islamic medicine, such as Ibn Sina (Avicenna), Al-Razi 
(Rhazes), and Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya, taught that the human being is 
created upon a delicate harmony of elements, qualities, and spiritual forces. 
This harmony is known as Mizaj (temperament). 
What is Mizaj?

What is Mizaj? 
Mizaj refers to the natural temperament or inner constitution of a person, organ, 
or substance. It results from the blending of four elemental qualities: 
•
Hot (ḥār) 
•
Cold (bārid) 
•
Moist (raṭb) 
•
Dry (yābis) 
Each human is born with a unique combination of these qualities, forming their 
personal temperament. Ibn Sina writes:

Prophetic Medicine and the Concept of Balance 
In Tibb an-Nabawi (Prophetic Medicine), the Messenger of Allah ﷺ 
emphasised moderation and balance in food, sleep, emotions, and worship. He 
ﷺ said: 
“The son of Adam does not fill any vessel worse than his stomach… A few

morsels are sufficient for him to keep his back straight.” 
(Tirmidhi) 
This hadith is not only spiritual advice, it is a medical principle: overeating 
creates imbalance in the mizaj, weakens digestion, and leads to disease.

M A R R I A G E I N I S L A M I C M E D I C I N E ) 
Marriage (nikāh) in Islam is not only a legal contract but a union of bodies, 
minds, and souls. Just as the body has a unique mizaj (temperament), each 
spouse brings their own physical, emotional, and spiritual temperament into the 
marriage. Harmony occurs when these temperaments complement one another; 
conflict arises when they greatly oppose or remain unbalanced.

“And among His signs is that He created for you spouses from among 
yourselves, that you may find tranquillity (sakinah) in them, and He 
placed between you love and mercy.” 
(Qur'an 30:21) 
2. What is Mizaj in Marriage? 
Mizaj relates to: 
•
Body (Hot, Cold, Dry, Moist) 
•
Personality / Emotions (anger, calmness, sadness, excitement) 
•
Spiritual State (patience, ego, humility, awareness of Allah) 
When two people marry, their mizaj interact physically, emotionally, and 
spiritually.

spiritually.

5. How to Balance with Your Spouse 
2 7 6
            C O P Y R I G H T © A I S H A D A H I R

Allah created pairs not to mirror each other, but to complete each other’s 
balance. Understanding your spouse’s mizaj turns that frustration into 
compassion. 
Prophetic principle: 
“The best of you are those who are best to their spouses.” (Tirmidhī) 
Temperamental opposites can create equilibrium when handled with gentleness. 
Where one burns, the other cools. Where one freezes, the other stirs movement. 
Marriage is thus a divine ecosystem,  the emotional mizāj of two souls striving

for harmony under Allah. 
6. Healing the Inner Climate 
Every imbalance begins in the soul before it appears in the body. 
•
The fiery soul must practice sabr (patience). 
•
The cold soul must renew shukr (gratitude). 
•
The dry heart must seek tears in sujūd. 
•
The moist heart must learn discipline in worship.

Moderation is the sunnah of the body and the path of the heart. 
“The most beloved of deeds to Allah are those done consistently, even if little.” 
(Bukhārī) 
“And the earth—We spread it out and caused everything to grow therein 
in due measure.” (Qur’an 15:19) 
Balance is Allah’s signature. The same law that keeps the stars in orbit governs 
the chemistry of your blood. To heal is not to suppress symptoms, but to return

to divine proportion  where heat meets coolness, dryness meets moisture, and 
the heart finds peace between effort and tawakkul. 
That is Ash-Shifāʾ: the equilibrium of body, mind, and soul.
